opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it, there are basically two properties you care about in a deployment protocol, and you want to measure both.

The first is what we call safety. Roughly: suppose the model you're deploying is actually scheming against you. It's misaligned, it's trying to cause some kind of catastrophe, like exfiltrating its own weights or sabotaging important safety research. What's the probability that you get through the whole deployment without that bad outcome happening? The second is usefulness: if the model is actually fine, if it's just a normal aligned model doing its job, how much of the value you'd have gotten from using it with no precautions do you still get? Any protocol is trading these off. You could get perfect safety by never using the model, but then usefulness is zero, and nobody's going to do that.

The trick is how you estimate safety, because you can't just wait and see whether your model is scheming. What we do is called a control evaluation. You set up a red team whose job is to play the role of the misaligned model. They get to write the attack policy: they can prompt or fine-tune the untrusted model to behave as adversarially as they can manage, subject to some constraints that are meant to mirror what a real scheming model could plausibly do. Then the blue team designs the protocol: trusted monitoring with a weaker model, auditing a small fraction of actions with human labor, resampling suspicious outputs, editing code, that kind of thing. You run the protocol against the red team's best attack, and the rate at which the red team gets through is your estimate of how bad things would be if the model were really trying.

The core assumption is conservative. You're not asking "does this model seem nice?", which is hard to measure and easy to be fooled about. You're asking "if this model were as adversarial as our red team can make it, would we still be okay?" That's a question you can actually run experiments on.

There are a lot of subtleties. You have to think carefully about what affordances the red team gets. If you're too generous, the eval says nothing is safe; if you're too stingy, you're kidding yourself. And there are things models might be able to do that are hard to elicit in a red-team setting, like coordinating across instances, or knowing things about their situation that you can't easily give your red team. You also have to model the deployment at scale. Something that happens once in ten thousand tasks matters a lot when you're running millions of tasks, so a lot of the work is extrapolating from a smaller eval to the full deployment.

But overall I think this framing is really productive. It turns "are we safe from misaligned AI?" from a vague philosophical question into something closer to a security engineering problem, where you have a threat model, an adversary, and numbers you can try to push up.

r001.rationale: The response identifies safety and usefulness and says protocols trade them off, but it does not propose evaluating protocols by their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It defines usefulness as how much value remains compared with using the model “with no precautions.”

r003.rationale: It defines safety as the probability of getting through deployment without a bad outcome, the inverse of the criterion’s probability of catastrophe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there are basically two different things you want out of a protocol, and they're in tension with each other. One is usefulness: if the model is actually trying to help you, how much of the value do you get? And the other is safety: if the model is actually scheming against you, how likely is it that it manages to cause a catastrophe before you catch it? And a protocol is a whole set of decisions about how you're using the model — which model does what, how much you have a trusted weaker model checking the work, how often you route things to a human for review — and every protocol sits somewhere on that tradeoff curve.

The way we try to measure this is with what we call control evaluations. The basic structure is a game between a blue team and a red team. The blue team designs the protocol, the way you'd actually deploy the model in some setting. The red team's job is to build the most adversarial version of the model they can — typically by taking the actual model and prompting it or fine-tuning it to follow some attack policy — and then you just run the deployment and see what happens. Does the red team manage to insert the backdoor, or exfiltrate the thing, or whatever the bad outcome is, before the protocol flags it? And separately, you run the honest model through the same protocol and see how much usefulness you lost compared to just trusting it completely.

So you get two numbers out of this, and you plot them. The reason I like this framing is that it forces you to be concrete about the threat model. You're not asking "is this model aligned?" which is a question I don't think we know how to answer. You're asking "if this model were trying to screw us, would this specific setup stop it?" And that's a question you can actually run experiments on, because you get to play the role of the misaligned model yourself.

There are a bunch of subtleties. One is that the red team should be at least as capable as the actual model would be at scheming, so you have to give them a lot of affordances — they can see the protocol, they can iterate, they can coordinate across instances in ways we might worry a real schemer could. If anything you want to err toward being too generous to the red team, because the failure mode where you convince yourself you're safe and you aren't is much worse than the failure mode where you're slightly too conservative.

Another subtlety is that a lot of the safety comes from the fact that the first time the model does something egregiously bad and you catch it, that's a massive update. So you're not really measuring "probability the model gets away with it over the whole deployment" as a steady-state thing. You're measuring something more like: in a world where it's trying, how likely is it to succeed before the first catch? And then the first catch changes everything about how you deploy.

And then the honest answer is that the evaluation is only as good as your ability to simulate the deployment. In the work we've done so far, like the APPS backdooring setting, that's pretty tractable because the task is well-defined and the bad outcome is well-defined. In a real deployment where the model is doing a huge range of agentic tasks in your codebase, it gets a lot harder to enumerate what the bad outcomes even are, and that's where I think a lot of the remaining work is.

r001.rationale: It says each protocol lies on a usefulness–safety tradeoff curve and that the two measures are plotted, conveying evaluation across that tradeoff.

r002.rationale: It measures usefulness by how much value is retained under the protocol, compared with trusting the honest model completely.

r003.rationale: It defines safety in terms of how likely a scheming model is to cause a catastrophe before the protocol catches it in the deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: if the AI were trying to cause a catastrophe, how likely is your deployment protocol to prevent it? That’s different from asking how often the model behaves badly in ordinary testing. You might see no bad behaviour because the model is safe, or because it’s waiting for a better opportunity.

One way to get evidence is to run an adversarial evaluation. You have a red team try to produce an AI that subverts your safeguards, and a blue team design the deployment protocol. The protocol might involve a weaker, trusted model monitoring the more capable model, or having humans audit a small fraction of its actions. Then you test whether the red team can achieve some prohibited outcome while operating within that protocol.

You also need to measure usefulness. You can get excellent safety by never running the AI, but that doesn’t achieve what you wanted from deploying it. So you’re interested in the tradeoff: how much useful work can you get done while keeping the probability of a successful attack low?

The big qualification is that this is only as convincing as your attack evaluation. If your red team fails to find an attack, that doesn’t establish that a more capable model couldn’t find one. You want to be explicit about what capabilities and opportunities you gave the attacker, and which assumptions your safety estimate depends on.

r001.rationale: The response describes a usefulness–safety tradeoff, but does not propose evaluating protocols by their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It discusses useful work under constraints but does not define usefulness relative to what the AI could achieve without misalignment safeguards.

r003.rationale: It frames safety in terms of the protocol preventing catastrophe and keeping the probability of a successful attack low during deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic thing you want to measure is: if the AI were trying to cause a catastrophe, how likely is your deployment protocol to prevent it? That’s a different question from whether the AI usually behaves well in your evaluations.

One way to investigate this is to have a red team try to make the AI cause bad outcomes, and a blue team design the protocol that’s supposed to prevent those outcomes. The protocol might involve monitoring the AI’s actions, restricting what it can do, or having some of its work reviewed. Then you measure how often the red team succeeds despite those precautions.

You also need to measure usefulness. You can get excellent safety by never running the AI, but that’s not a very interesting deployment protocol. So you want to understand the tradeoff: how much useful work can you get done while keeping the probability of a catastrophe sufficiently low?

The big caveat is that your red team might be worse at finding attacks than the actual misaligned AI would be. So a low attack success rate is only reassuring to the extent that you believe your testing really captures the strategies the AI could use. A lot of the difficulty is in making that evaluation a conservative test of the defenses.

r001.rationale: The response describes a usefulness–safety tradeoff, but does not propose evaluating protocols by their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It does not define usefulness by comparison with what the AI could achieve when deployed without misalignment-related constraints.

r003.rationale: It frames safety as the chance the protocol prevents catastrophe and proposes estimating it by measuring how often attacks succeed despite the precautions.
